title: Dynamic quantification anti‑fraud machine learning model for real‑time transaction fraud detection in banking
tldr: Introduces a dynamic quantification anti-fraud model combining F-Beta features with a double machine learning framework for real-time transaction risk assessment and deployed in a banking production environment.
problem_and_motivation: Traditional anti-fraud models relying on expert rules or machine learning suffer from poor real-time performance, high false positive rates, and computational intensity that hinders proactive fraud prevention. There is a need for a model that can perform instantaneous risk assessments on massive transaction volumes while maintaining accuracy and adapting to evolving fraud tactics.
approach: Defines 20+ expert rules as binary features based on suspicious transaction behaviors from historical fraud patterns.
Computes F-Beta scores for each feature with beta=3 to prioritize recall over precision.
Applies a double machine learning (DML) framework with LightGBM and XGBoost to quantify causal feature weights and reduce collinearity.
Uses logarithmic transformation to normalize F-Beta value distributions and prevent high-frequency features from dominating.
Implements a regularization penalty function based on daily complaints and leads to reduce false positives.
Dynamically adjusts risk thresholds based on branch processing capacity and complaint rates for operational feasibility.
Deploys the model in a real-time streaming architecture with 5-10 second latency per transaction.
Evaluates using a test set of 633 implicated cards and production metrics including bank ranking and proportion of involved cards.
Compares performance against XGBoost and expert rule baselines using recall, FPR, F1-score, and cost metrics.
Conducts post-deployment monitoring over six months to measure long-term impact on fraud reduction.
findings: num: Validation sample recall rate reached 0.506 on 633 test positive samples.
num: Post-deployment, the bank's proportion of implicated cards reduced by 30 percentage points (from 50% to 20%) within six months.
num: The bank's province-wide ranking for involved cards dropped from 1st to 4th place.
num: F1-score of the dynamic model ranges from 0.32 to 0.38, compared to 0.28-0.34 for XGBoost.
num: False positive rate for the dynamic model is 0.15-0.20, versus 0.25-0.35 for XGBoost.
num: Operational cost reduced by 30-40% compared to XGBoost due to fewer false positives.
num: The model generated 170,594 potentially involved card clues from September 2023 to March 2024.
num: Processing latency is 5-10 seconds per transaction versus minutes for traditional machine learning.
num: Customer complaint rate decreased by 40% post-deployment.

Figure 3: Nominal distribution probability density versus F-beta value curve → justifies log transformation to normalize skewed feature distributions.
Table 1: F-beta values for 21 implicated card features in June 2023 → shows feature performance variation and supports weight quantification.
Table 2: Real-time performance comparison of expert rules, XGBoost, and dynamic model → demonstrates latency and throughput advantages.
Table 3: Core performance metrics comparing dynamic model, XGBoost, and expert rules → quantifies recall, FPR, F1, and cost improvements.
Table 4: Long-term impact metrics six months post-deployment → shows reduction in involved card proportion, rank, and complaints.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes a novel dynamic quantification anti-fraud model that combines F-Beta feature scoring, double machine learning for causal weight estimation, and real-time streaming architecture for transaction fraud detection. It demonstrates a practical deployment in a banking production environment, showing significant reduction in implicated card proportions and bank ranking among peers. The model addresses the gap between computationally intensive machine learning and the need for real-time transaction interception. It also provides an industry-relevant evaluation framework using macro-level bank performance indicators rather than isolated test-set metrics.
directly_justifies: Traditional anti-fraud models have poor real-time performance and high false positive rates.
Machine learning algorithms struggle with vast transaction volumes due to computational intensity.
The dynamic model achieves 5-10 second latency for real-time transaction interception.
Post-deployment, the bank's involved card proportion dropped from 50% to 20%.
Dynamic weight adjustment via DML reduces bias from correlated features.
limits: Potential dataset bias exists due to oversampling and selection criteria focusing on low-asset accounts.
Generalizability is constrained as the model relies predominantly on transaction data and neglects demographic, social media, and device data.
Balanced dataset design does not reflect real-world fraud rarity, risking overfitting to synthetic data.
Normal accounts selected using same thresholds as positive samples may contain borderline risk cases, contaminating the control group.
No external validation using datasets from other banks or regions is reported.
